title: Community-based coproduction of knowledge about wildlife trade and anthrax as a high-consequence pathogen
content:
Abstract
The illegal wildlife trade is a dynamic, transnational form of environmental crime that intersects with numerous socioeconomic and public health issues. Despite increased global efforts to combat the illegal wildlife trade, significant gaps with implications for prevention exist in understanding plausible links among the illegal wildlife trade, traditional medicine, zoonotic diseases, and wildlife conservation. In this article, we review threat reduction for environment, people, and animals (TREPA) research, which explores the intersections of the illegal wildlife trade, anthrax, and traditional medicine within portions of the Greater Limpopo Transfrontier Conservation Area. TREPA's approach involved knowledge coproduction through an indaba, a traditional African method for decision-making. The TREPA indaba helped advance large-team science and community coproduction of knowledge about appropriate research methodologies, strengthened preparedness, and suggested response strategies. The indaba is one model that could be adapted and applied to other contexts, leveraging the benefits of community-centered research methods in addressing global challenges such as those associated with One Health.
